author: rti_admin
title: The Ahmedabad Reading Controversy and the Freedom to Read
content:
Who gets to decide what we should read? The question arose sharply in Ahmedabad this August, when two books were removed from a school reading list, and a silent reading session was later disrupted.

In August, an Ahmedabad school removed Malala Yousafzai’s I Am Malala and Anne Frank’s The Diary of a Young Girl from its reading list after objections from some parents and protests involving right-wing organisations. Later that month, a silent reading session organised in Vastrapur was reportedly disrupted by a group claiming affiliation with the Vishwa Hindu Parishad and Bajrang Dal. The gathering included students, lawyers, media professionals and others. The reading itself became the object of confrontation.

I Am Malala is the memoir of a girl who survived an assassination attempt after publicly advocating girls’ right to education. The Diary of a Young Girl records the experiences of a Jewish teenager hiding from Nazi persecution before Anne Frank died during the Holocaust. Whatever one thinks of Malala’s political views, or of the ways her story is interpreted, reading her memoir does not require accepting every view she holds. Anne Frank’s diary similarly allows readers to encounter the testimony of a young person caught inside one of history’s greatest crimes.

A book is not a political membership card.

Reading allows a person to encounter an argument without accepting it. A reader can examine its evidence, question its assumptions and reject its conclusions. The point is that judgement becomes possible through encounter.

Education is often described as the transmission of knowledge. But knowledge without the capacity to question it can become another form of conformity.

This question of who may read and what they may encounter carries a specific weight in the Indian context. For much of India’s history, access to formal education was deeply shaped by caste hierarchy. Ambedkar wrote that under the Chaturvarna system, the right to education was assigned to the Brahmins, Kshatriyas and Vaishyas, while Shudras were denied it. He also discussed the denial of education to women. The control of education was therefore connected to the wider system of graded inequality that Ambedkar analysed.

This was one of the structures challenged by Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule. Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule opened a school for girls in Pune in 1848, and Phule later set up schools for the Mahars and Mangs. In his 1882 testimony before the Education Commission, Phule criticised the concentration of education among the higher classes and called for a wider spread of primary and female education. His educational work treated access to knowledge as a social question rather than a privilege confined to a small section of society.

Dr B.R. Ambedkar’s conception of democracy makes this problem especially important. In Annihilation of Caste, he imagined an ideal society with “varied and free points of contact with other modes of association” and described democracy as “a mode of associated living.” For Ambedkar, fraternity was not sameness. It required people to participate in a common social world despite their differences. His writings on the Depressed Classes emerged from a context in which these communities faced restrictions on access to public wells and schools, and were subjected to social segregation and prescribed occupations. The “associated living” he imagined presupposes that those who were once excluded from classrooms are now full participants in the world of ideas.

A democratic society cannot expect citizens to form independent judgements while continually narrowing the range of ideas they are permitted to encounter. The democratic reader needs the freedom to examine an argument before deciding whether it deserves acceptance, rejection or further examination.

John Dewey understood education as inseparable from democratic life. For Dewey, democracy depended on communication, inquiry and shared experience. He saw education as a way of preparing people to participate intelligently in common life.

Not every book belongs in every classroom. Parents can question reading lists, teachers can challenge texts, and schools can make decisions about age, pedagogy and context. Citizens can protest. A democratic society must leave room for disagreement over education. The important distinction is between arguing that a book should not be taught and intimidating people who choose to read it. The first concerns the content and place of a text in education. The second makes the act of reading itself a political offence.

Contemporary concerns about caste discrimination in higher education, including its relationship to student distress and suicides, remain serious enough to have been examined by the Supreme Court-appointed National Task Force on student mental health and suicides.

The harder democratic principle is to defend the reader’s freedom even when we dislike the book being read. Otherwise, “intellectual freedom” simply becomes another name for allowing ideas with which we already agree.

This is why the Ahmedabad episode matters beyond the two books involved. The deeper question is who gets to decide what a citizen may encounter before that citizen has had the opportunity to form a judgement.

Once reading itself becomes evidence of political allegiance, we begin judging the person who has chosen to read a book rather than only the ideas within it. “What does this book say?” becomes “What does reading this book say about you?” The reader is then placed on trial alongside the ideas in the book.

A society that makes the second question more important than the first risks producing citizens who know which ideas belong to their side but have little opportunity to examine ideas outside that boundary.

The people who gathered for the silent reading session in Vastrapur had come to read. They were exercising their judgement through the simple act of sitting with books.

A democratic citizen should be free to encounter an idea, question it, and decide what to make of it. In India, defending that freedom is inseparable from defending the right of readers from the Depressed Classes and other communities historically excluded from education to full and equal access to the world of texts.

Rajat Kanti Satpati is an author of several books. His writing has appeared in SteinbeckNow, People’s Daily, and other publications.

author: rti_admin
title: The Questions of Milinda: Publisher’s Note on Navayana Edition
content:
A river remains alive only so long as fresh water continues to flow through it. The same principle applies to language. Language is never static; it evolves with time. Its vocabulary, sentence structure, and modes of expression continually change. Whether one considers Hindi, English, or any other language, it becomes evident that literature written in the nineteenth century is often difficult for contemporary readers to approach without assistance.

For this reason, responsible publishers of classical literature frequently present ancient works in a renewed form, adapting their language, style, and presentation to the needs of modern readers. Such efforts enable timeless ideas to remain accessible to new generations.

When we turn to Buddhist literature, however, we find that relatively little attention has been given to this task. Many texts continue to be published in styles that remain largely unchanged from earlier translations. Regrettably, this has contributed to an increasing distance between younger readers and the rich intellectual heritage of Buddhism.

One remarkable work that has suffered from this situation is the Milinda Pañha (Questions of King Milinda). This extraordinary text preserves a series of profound dialogues between King Milinda and Venerable Nāgasena, offering readers an accessible gateway into the heart of Buddhist philosophy through reasoned inquiry and debate.

Today, this book can be found in many Buddhist households across India. Yet experience suggests that, although it occupies a place of honour on many bookshelves, it is seldom read in its entirety. Many readers begin it with enthusiasm but fail to complete it. This is not mere excuse-making; it is a practical reality. The difficulty arises largely from an archaic style of translation and a language that often feels distant from contemporary readers.

As publishers, we felt it insufficient merely to lament this situation. Instead, we resolved to seek a constructive solution. Our volume, The Questions of Milinda: Milindapañha in Navayana Perspective, represents the second step in that endeavour. The first was Navayāna Darśana: A Modern Interpretation of the Buddha’s Teachings, which presented Buddhist philosophy in a simple, rational, and contemporary style. The enthusiastic response it received, leading it nearly to go out of print, encouraged us to continue this work.

The present book is not a direct translation of the original Pāli text. Rather, it is a careful reworking based upon a comparative study of English, Hindi, and, to some extent, Marathi translations. Many existing versions contain accounts of previous births and other traditional elements that appear difficult to reconcile with modern scientific understanding and with claims concerning the rational and humanistic character of Buddhist philosophy.

In this edition, Author Ratnesh Katulkar has sought to remove such accretions and reinterpret the text through a Navayāna perspective, presenting it in a clear, modern, and accessible form for contemporary readers. Yet this undertaking presented a significant challenge. The original questions of Milinda and the replies of Nāgasena could neither be arbitrarily expanded nor fundamentally altered. How, then, could they be made more approachable?

The solution adopted was both simple and effective. The original dialogues have been preserved with only minimal modifications, mainly involving language and presentation. However, following nearly every question-and-answer exchange, explanatory sections have been added in which the discussion is interpreted afresh in the light of modern knowledge and contemporary concerns. In this way, the text has been connected to present realities while preserving the spirit of the original dialogue.

We are confident that this approach will appeal both to readers already interested in Buddhist philosophy and to newcomers seeking an accessible introduction to the Dhamma.

It is only natural, however, that some readers deeply attached to traditional interpretations and inherited assumptions may not feel entirely comfortable with this presentation. Any attempt to revisit established traditions is often met with resistance. Yet the Buddha’s path itself is one of inquiry, reflection, and continuous investigation. Following the spirit of the Kālāma Sutta, it encourages individuals to examine truth for themselves rather than accept doctrines solely based on authority or tradition.

Our purpose is not to provoke those committed to conventional views, but to ensure that younger generations become active participants in the Buddhist intellectual heritage. For that reason, it is perhaps best to pay little attention to reactionary criticism. Navayāna, after all, resembles an elephant that continues steadily on its path without being distracted by passing noises. This book is simply another step in that journey.

History repeatedly demonstrates that every significant intellectual and social transformation faced opposition in its own time. Yet it is often these very transformations that later shape the course of human civilisation. Generations afterwards, historians frequently look back with surprise at the resistance such movements encountered.

Navayāna is part of that continuing tradition of renewal. The flame first kindled by the Buddha illuminated vast regions of the world in the age of Emperor Aśoka. Though dimmed during periods of decline and reaction, it was rekindled in modern times by figures such as P. Lakshmi Narasu, Dharmanand Kosambi, and Dr B. R. Ambedkar, inspiring countless thinkers and reformers across the world. Each of these individuals encountered hostility from conservative circles; therefore, criticism of our own efforts should come as no surprise. Indeed, our author often remarks that a positive mind can transform even hostility and irritation into a source of strength and motivation.

This book was not written in isolation. The entire manuscript was taught and discussed online with students over an extended period. Every dialogue, criticism, observation, and suggestion emerging from those discussions was carefully considered and incorporated where appropriate. The final text was subsequently reviewed and approved by the wider Navayāna study group. Consequently, this volume should not be viewed merely as the private opinion of its author. It is, rather, a collective expression shaped through dialogue, study, reflection, and collaboration among the students of Navayāna. We sincerely hope that readers will find it worthy of their expectations.

We humbly request all readers to share their reflections, suggestions, and critical assessments after reading this book. Your thoughtful responses will guide and inspire our future work.

Book Title: The Questions of Milinda: Milindapañha in Navayana Perspective

Publisher: Navayana Prakashan, Nasik

author: rti_admin
title: The IITs: Tragic Failures That Beget More Tragedies
content:
From a social perspective, the IITs are tragic failures that beget more tragedies.

But you already know the IITs are the pinnacle of Indian aspirations, achievements, accolades, blah-di-blah, right? How about we celebrate by taking a closer look at the graduates, the faculty, and the institution?

The institutional charter, briefly. The IITs were conceived in 1946 to support the country’s industrial development and help meet the nation’s technological challenges. Parliament’s 1961 Act declares them institutions of national importance. It charges them with instruction and research, and with the advancement of learning and dissemination of knowledge. The same Act says every institute shall be open to persons of either sex and of whatever race, creed, caste or class, in admitting or appointing students and teachers alike. [1] Later laws reserve seats for SC, ST and OBC students, PhD seats included, and, since 2019, teaching posts at every rank.

Start with the product. As any IIT alum would confirm, a majority of IIT graduates wouldn’t be able to properly describe what ‘engineering’ is. Poorly educated and narrowly conditioned to chase status from a young age, most of them used to end up in finance or as middle management in US IT firms, but have lately diversified into mercenary ouroboros via IIT coaching and YouTube influencing. The institute’s own numbers: in IIT Bombay’s placement report for 2023–24, 29% of offers were in engineering and technology. The rest went to IT, consulting, finance, analytics and “other”. [2]

The defence is usually the famous founders. Let’s do the math. Seats went from about 2k a year in the 80s to about 20k now, so total grads ~400k. Unicorn founders ~117, high value startup founders maybe four thousand if you’re generous. So, 0.03% and 1%. [3, 4] Like unicorns, these founders are statistical anomalies. Sensible folks within the system will themselves readily acknowledge that their success is mostly despite it rather than because of it. And given the stated mission, funnelling billions in public subsidy into private equity accumulation for a minuscule minority is cause for shame rather than something to tom-tom about.

This is the deal then. Ruin your childhood to join an exclusive band of svayambhu achievers. Concoct jagatguru-brand gig economy “innovations” for exploiting cheap labor. Garland each other for contributions to the economic miracle of jobless growth and extractive digital feudalism. Parade your arrogant indifference or offer defensive apologies for the mockery of a social contract, dressed up in a lazy pragmatism argument about success.

By the way, who’s even there to teach them? Across all 23 IITs, 4,804 of 12,498 sanctioned teaching posts stood vacant in January 2026, or 38.4%. [5] It was 38.3% in December 2022. [6] In the nine IITs that disclosed the breakdown, about 60% of the empty posts were reserved ones. [5] Cryogenic sthiratva.

Sour grapes? I was there, eating them for four lost years. So chill. First week in the hostel, the rank was a common icebreaker question you asked people along with where they were from and in what department. Some hesitant answers made me stop asking. Only the rare, confident stud would openly declare he was SC, came through the preparatory course etc. The term in use was ‘schaddu’, and people would murmur in the early semesters, but soon some of them were ahead on GPA, and the murmurs lost voice. Years later, a friend who got a PhD mentioned feeling conflicted using reservations since their father was also a PhD and they went to good schools. Not long ago, an alum stated that even though they got in via reservation, everything after was earned by merit. I couldn’t make out if this was being defensive or proud. I don’t remember hearing of any campus suicides, and only learned about them from ‘The Death of Merit’ documentary. [7]

A decade after graduation and on another continent, the sourness still stung, in an interview by another pitiable alum. I was struggling for purpose and careening across career lanes. Unusual for an IIT grad, and he got suspicious… maybe I was a ‘category candidate’? So he asked for my rank, and then I asked for his, and then he said that’s not relevant, and then I agreed, and the interview went downhill. So, no chill.

Then the people who run the place. Do the IITs still hire blatantly sexist dogs as professors? It used to be de rigueur in several departments. A lot of the students were of a similar breed, excusable perhaps for their youthful ignorance and terrible cultural milieu. (Apologies to the canines for this unfortunate figure of human speech.) Anyone who was there will attest to this. Women who studied at IIT Bombay in the 1970s and 80s wrote in 2021 that they had heard many sexist comments from their teachers. [8] And they still do hire them: in 2025, IIT Roorkee dismissed one of its senior-most professors after a complaint from his own PhD student. [9] In late 2024 IIT Mandi compulsorily retired a professor, who has appealed, after its complaints committee upheld sexual harassment charges brought by two BTech students. A different professor was accused and removed soon after. Neither case went to the police. [10] Note that the compulsory retirement leaves the retirement benefits in place.

Ok, coming to caste, proper. Can we hide from it anywhere in this sanskari culture? In a 2022 survey by IIT Bombay’s SC/ST Students’ Cell, over 37% of the 388 Dalit and Adivasi students who replied had been asked their rank by classmates fishing for their caste, and 77 reported discrimination from faculty and fellow students. [11] 18-year-old Darshan Solanki died there in February 2023. 22-year-old Sahil Wakode died there in September 2026. Both were Dalit, and both families allege caste discrimination. In the first case, the institute’s committee ruled it out. In the second, the police have an abetment case open under the Atrocities Act and a professor is suspended. [12] They are two of many: at least 120 IIT students died by suicide or other unnatural causes in the past decade, up from 51 in the one before, by an alumnus’s count from RTI replies and press reports. By his estimate, SC and ST students died by suicide at about twice the general rate. [13] Do your graveyard shift and choose between being horrified by the deaths and body counting by caste category.

And these worthies cannot find “suitable candidates” for reserved faculty posts. The law has required it at every rank since 2019. Asked how to comply, a committee of IIT directors recommended in 2020 that the IITs be exempted altogether. Their case was one standard for everyone, and candidates not good enough. Quota at entry if you must, but not at professor; no university abroad that competes for faculty carries such a thing. Ok, directors, abroad means not India. But no university abroad has a law telling it to be open to every caste. The IITs do. The ministry instead ordered the faculty posts filled by September 2022. [14]

The record since, from RTI replies obtained by the Ambedkar Periyar Phule Study Circle (APPSC) at IIT Bombay: of 412 full professors at IIT Bombay, none is ST, five are SC, and six are OBC; so 97% are general category. Among 363 associate and assistant professors, 29 are SC, eight ST and 35 OBC. [15] It is not for want of applicants: in 2023, 523 SC, 96 ST and 779 OBC candidates applied. Four were selected, all of them SC. [16, 17] So their own PhD pipeline has failed? Of the 25,007 PhD students the IITs admitted between 2015 and 2019, 9.1% were SC and 2.1% ST, against quotas of 15% and 7.5%. [18] At IIT Delhi in 2024, the faculty was 89.1% general category, 2.7% SC and 1.1% ST. [19]

Let’s swing by the apex gatekeepers. Is there caste data on the top administrative positions: directors, deans, HoDs? When you have a full professor pool that is 97% “general category” and “general” means “merit”, no need to ask about caste, only merit. Get it?

As Kuffir wrote back in 2012: “The general category is the seat of caste, not the reserved categories.” [20]

A parliamentary committee on SC/ST welfare, looking at central institutions in 2025, flagged the “suitable candidates not found” excuse. [21] Suitable for what? In the old IITs, dogs attended/slept in classes more regularly than the students. Of those who attended, maybe about 5% paid attention, 1% actually understood. These numbers sound ridiculous until you ask the IIT grads, or read IIT Bombay’s own surveys. In the institute’s 2017 stakeholder survey, 56% of the students who responded said there was no academic honesty among students, and faculty called copying and plagiarism rampant. [22] Earlier, the student magazine rated the place 5 out of 10 on academic integrity, with professors who know most of the class can’t answer a hard question, and courses diluted so the failures stay manageable. [23] The IITs brought in 75-85% attendance rules. But IIT Dhanbad scrapped its own in 2025 at its students’ request, because they were sitting in class only to mark attendance. [24]

All of the above has been written and spoken about. A lot. One can read Round Table India [25, 16] or watch the documentary online for free. [7] The meritorious can buy ‘The Caste of Merit’ book for Rs. 7,000. [26]

And the research? The charter asks for it, so look. In QS, where 45% of the score is two reputation surveys, the older IITs rank between 123 and 339 in the world. [27] In the Leiden ranking, which takes no submissions and counts only published papers, they rank between 874 and 1,309 of 1,594 on the share of their output among the world’s 10% most cited. [28] In Times Higher Education rankings, which weights research quality at 30%, they appear nowhere: seven of them stopped submitting in 2020, after placing between 401 and 800. [29] Leiden they cannot withdraw from. At home, in the ministry’s own NIRF ranking, built largely on data the institutes themselves submit, they are on top. [30]

So, the institution routinely fails its mission and charter, has crippling problems teaching and motivating those it admits, ranks in the world’s bottom half for research that matters, and has sustained, well-documented, and alleged discrimination against historically suppressed groups in both faculty and student bodies. But it svayam-ranks at the top at home, and remains prestigious.

None of this is an accident. The IITs were founded on a promise to be open to whatever caste. Then they recruit broadly and promote narrowly. The reserved students also pass the entrance and get the certificate, and the category follows them around the campus anyway. Their PhD seats go unfilled. At hiring, the full professors decide who is “suitable”. The elite keep the intruders in check by other means, and the costs are limited to the lower rungs. At every step, the judging is in their own hands.

So there are two possibilities. Either no suitable candidates exist, in which case institutes that have admitted SC and ST students for about fifty years, and award the PhDs themselves, have produced none. [31] Or they exist and are turned away, and 1,398 applicants and four selections at IIT Bombay in one year suggest where to look. Either way the promise is broken.

The gatekeepers call the yardstick merit, but the yardstick moves. A reserved student clears the entrance exam and earns the same degree, and is still asked for their rank. They earn the PhD, and are still “not found suitable” to be faculty. To the svayam-meritorious, reservations feel like a crowbar in the gate, a claw dug into the soft flesh of privilege. The promise gets broken – it was never theirs to keep – and it costs them nothing. The ministry’s deadline passed in 2022, and the numbers have not moved. The IITs are judged by who gets in and by their handful of unicorns, never by their charter. That is the gate: cold in its results, banal in its daily working, and consequence-free.

What is the solution then? The antireservationists should be granted their wish and reservations abolished. The resulting bonfire will burn everything to the ground and maybe allow for a more equitable reconstruction of this miserable society dominated by ignorant merit-my-foot mongers and their knowing but pathologically power-addicted cousins. The wish for the bonfire is theirs, though, not mine.

Caste is a lucrative, subliminal corruption of the soul, beyond the reach of arguments, which are cheap to ignore. The cure is cost: capability, power, consequence, and relentlessness. The reservations, the graduates, the PhDs are proof of battles already won. So are the RTIs: most of the numbers above were pried out by students, APPSC at IIT Bombay above all, not handed over. The counter strategy of the savarna elites is to manage and mitigate the costs at lower levels. So, not first and then. Claim rights in situ and also build further where their gates aren’t allowed by design, in independent institutions.

Until the cost hurts, the suicides go on, the posts stay empty, the charter is in tatters. But hey, the prestige stays intact!

Who wins? Not the dead. Not the humiliated who stay. Not the IIT grad who got a rank and no purpose. Not the genuine teachers trapped inside. Not society.

Save your tears, stay blind and celebrate.

author: rti_admin
title: No, not the Generation: Political Mobilisation and Changing Grammar of Protest in India
content:
Both academic and non-academic spheres are recurrently using terms like “Gen-Z protest,” “Gen Z’s political anger,” “Gen Z pressure,” “Gen-Z consciousness,” and “Gen Z politics” to describe the follow-up events. US public broadcaster NPR, despite accentuating the statistics of joblessness and inequality across South Asia as latent sources of unrest, concludes its argument by portraying “Gen Z” as an active political force. I feel some edginess with how a demographic detail is so readily treated as an explanation, when it is, at best, merely a description. Young people marching in large numbers, staging sit-ins, occupying public spaces, and facing tear gas are not new phenomena of 2026. These have long been a persistent feature of political activism in India. For instance, Bhagat Singh’s Naujawan Bharat Sabha (1926) had already demonstrated the political mobilization of youth nearly a century before.

Protests against exam-leaks are not new to India. We witnessed similar protests regarding the NEET exam in 2024. However, in 2026 the movement evolved into a mass youth mobilization, garnering national and international attention. It was driver not solely due to the examination scandal, but its collision with an unrelated event. author: rti_admin
title: Her life ended in one night. Her justice is still in the queue
content:
“Who will answer?” And “We cheered because the courts made us wait!”

Every rape case begins with a person: a daughter, a sister, a mother who trusted the road home. The numbers can feel cold, but they are made of lives, and any honest conversation has to carry both the data and the grief.

In November 2025, the World Health Organization and its UN partners released their most comprehensive estimates yet on violence against women (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240116962). Approximately 840 million women, nearly one in three, have experienced partner or sexual violence in their lifetime, and the rate has barely changed in 25 years (https://www.who.int/news/item/19-11-2025-lifetime-toll–840-million-women-faced-partner-or-sexual-violence). For the first time the report also estimated sexual violence by someone other than a partner: approximately 263 million women have experienced it since age 15 (https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/violence-against-women). Experts caution that this figure is significantly under-reported because of stigma and fear (https://www.who.int/news/item/19-11-2025-lifetime-toll–840-million-women-faced-partner-or-sexual-violence).

author: rti_admin
title: Why do we Protest? A Moral and Philosophical Basis
content:
The protests that have sparked in most South Asian countries in the last few years have sparked hope for socio-political, economic, and cultural change. Bangladesh’s protest over the job crisis in 2024, Nepal’s Gen Z protest (2025), and Sri Lanka’s protest of 2022 shocked the nations and their corrupt political systems. The Gen Z protest forced ruling BJP minister Dharmendra Pradhan in India to resign and raised demands for educational reform and accountability in 2026. The growing unrest of youths and their protests demand an objective analysis. This article asks some fundamental questions on the moral, philosophical, existential, and political basis of protest. More than answering the question of why we protest, this article is about why we should protest. While the outward manifestation and result of protest are obvious, the inward changes that protest brings are pertinent in shaping the morale of individuals in particular and society in general.

Let us ask, therefore, why shall we protest? Do we protest because we are bad? Bad as citizens, bad as human beings, bad daughters, and sons? Why do our youth protest? Why does this act of protest arouse so much fear? Fear from society and the state. author: rti_admin
title: The Algorithm of the Ballot: How Data Decides Democracy Before We Vote
content:
Elections used to be loud. Street-corner rallies, hoarse loudspeakers, campaigners going door to door, entire neighbourhoods gathered around a television for the evening debate. That version of democracy is dying, and most of us haven’t quite noticed the funeral. The real contest now happens somewhere quieter — inside a smartphone screen, in the space between a thumb and a feed. Political persuasion doesn’t shout at crowds anymore. It whispers to individuals, one at a time, and the whisper has been tested, refined, and timed with a precision no rally could ever match.

This isn’t speculation about some AI-run future. It’s already part of how political communication works in India and elsewhere with widespread mobile internet access.

Campaigns describe their own methods as “smart” and “surgical,” and for once the marketing language is accurate. Nobody is addressing an anonymous mass anymore. Every voter is a profile being built in real time — every scroll, every pause, every like or skip can become another data point feeding a model of who you are and what might move you. Linger two seconds longer on a video about unemployment, and your feed may begin showing you more content like it, each one worded slightly differently, until what started as manufactured content starts to feel like your own settled opinion.

author: rti_admin
title: Caste Denied, Gender Dismissed: Reading Literature, Love and Social Life through Selective Lenses
content:
Literature both reflects and shapes social life. This article examines how literature, people’s perspectives, and social life are deeply entangled. It asks how literary works and social relations are interpreted through selective lenses that foreground some forms of inequality while obscuring others. What readers notice in a literary work is not always separate from how they understand the social world around them. Their interpretations are shaped by what they recognise as important, what they have experienced, and what they may have learned to overlook. In this sense, reading is not simply an individual act of interpretation; it can also reveal how social inequalities are recognised, denied, or made invisible. Caste is denied in the name of progress and demanded in the name of awareness, while gender is dismissed in the name of unity. Through reflection on a poem and everyday experiences, this article shows how caste and patriarchy are intertwined rather than operating separately. Ignoring this reality reveals how easily we refuse to confront forms of inequality that do not directly affect us.
